quote: Even Harry Potter is superior to the Bible, both as a work of literary art and as moral philosophy.
content: This is a split verdict. On moral philosophy the essay has a stated criterion, the one in Harris's line: "coherent and compassionate." Against that criterion the comparison can be made and comes out as the essay says. One text regulates the buying and bequeathing of slaves (Leviticus 25:44–46) and commands the killing of Amalekite infants (1 Samuel 15:3). The other has an unkindness to house-elves that its own plot condemns. On literary art Fable is right. Auerbach is a real search, the essay's ranking is not, and "Ooh, shiny" in reverse is a fair diagnosis of that half of the sentence. The essay's method catches its own flourish, and the method still holds.

quote: It’s improbable that you used mistaken reasoning, yet made no mistakes.
content: The essay's claim concerns processes that are "unrelated" and "indefensible." Its example is "Ooh, shiny" standing in for dice. Take-the-best is neither of those. It works because it follows cue validities, which are the criterion's own structure, and expert intuition is valid when the environment is regular and the expert has had practice with feedback (Kahneman & Klein 2009). Those are processes Y correlated with X, and the dice sentence explicitly exempts them: "If you don't think that rolling dice would have been likely to produce the correct answer." The narrower suspicion Fable proposes, a justification built after the fact by someone with a stake, is the scenario the essay spells out: "since then, you've decided that you really ought to spend your money in such fashion..." The dice analogy does not conflate the two cases. It is aimed at that one.

quote: The standard atheist reply is given by Sam Harris: “You and I both know that it would take us five minutes to produce a book that offers a more coherent and compassionate morality than the Bible does.”
content: The claim answered is the one the essay reports. "Many Christians who've stopped really believing now insist that they revere the Bible as a source of ethical advice." Harris answers the claim as it was stated. Fable's reconstruction, that the reverence is a social and identity commitment and not an ethical judgment, is the essay's thesis: the stated justification is not the real one. That is what "Fake Justification" means. Fable and the essay agree that the ethical-advice justification was written above a bottom line put there by community and upbringing. The disagreement is only over whether that commitment is worth keeping, and the essay does not claim to have settled that.
